newsitem.title: FRANCE: Horse racing-Stars are born at Longchamp.
newsitem.headline: Horse racing-Stars are born at Longchamp.

text.p: Two stars were confirmed at Longchamp on Sunday -- one equine and one human.
Those lucky enough to see Olivier Peslier steer Helissio to a dazzling five length victory in the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe knew they had witnessed something special.
The winning margin could have been virtually doubled had Peslier chosen. Instead, understandably, the young Frenchman rose from the saddle to salute the crowd and his gallant partner.

The margin of superiority over second placed Pilsudski was just a length less than the great-Sea Bird recorded back in 1965 and only Ribot, who won the Arc twice in the 1950s, can boast similar prowess.

It may be early to jump to conclusions but few will forget the astonishing burst of acceleration shown by Helissio in the Longchamp finishing straight. The victory was all the more remarkable since the colt, a well backed favourite, had made virtually every metre of the running.

Queued up behind him were no less than four classic winners from around Europe plus a host of other top class performers. But none was allowed to get within reach once Peslier put the foot on the accelerator.

Pilsudki, ridden by Walter Swinburn, who had raced most of the 12-furlong (2.4 kms) trip upside Helissio did well to plug on in second place just ahead of the fast finishing Oscar Schindler, the mount of Cash Asmussen.

When Helissio won his Arc preparatory race, the Prix Niel over the course and distance last month, he was said to be only 80 percent fit. On Sunday there was no doubting that trainer Elie Lellouche had the colt in perfect trim to run the race of his life.
The only blot on an otherwise brilliant record is the French Derby when, ridden by Dominque Boeuf, Helissio fought to much for his head and flopped out of contention.

In his subsequent races, with Peslier on board, the colt has been alllowed to do as he wishes, and in the Arc he clearly wanted to make the running which was achieved to devastating effect. It was Peslier's first Arc success but others surely await for a young man who has already made a large impression on both sides of the English channel.
Peslier said "This is the greatest day of my life and this horse is the best.
"It was very easy. He controlled the race. It was almost as if the other jockeys stopped their horses for me!"
Trainer Lellouche and Spanish owner Enrique Sarasola were also winning the great race for the first time.
Sarasola, chairman of Madrid racetrack, turned down a six million sterling offer from Japan for Helissio before the Arc and his value will soar following his Arc win.
Still for sale, the colt looks destined for the Far East anyway with Lellouche favouring a trip to the Japan Cup over the Breeders' Cup in Canada.
While it was a great day for the French, the main English challenge proved to be disappointing.

Classic Cliche, ridden by man of the moment Frankie Dettori, found the pace to hot, Epsom Derby winner Shaamit, the mount of Pat Eddery, never got in a blow and Pentire, the King George VI and Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Stakes winner found the going too soft for his liking.
And the Peter Chapple-Hyam trained Polaris Flight, the mount of John Reid, had to be destroyed after breaking a leg.
Pentire's jockey Michael Hills observed succinctly "The winner had the race under control from seven furlongs (1.4 kms) out." Not many horses do that in the Arc.
